To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we found functionally specific changes in resting-state networks in motor learning that are related to either motor or perceptual learning.
we identified functionally specific changes in functional connectivity of resting-state sensorimotor networks after motor learning.
motor learning is associated with functionally specific changes in resting-state networks that are related to both motor and perceptual changes that accompany learning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms underlying the learning of motor skills.
understanding how learning changes the brain and how the brain is changed by learning.
the functional and structural changes that occur in the brain in association with learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the motor learning process is a dynamic process that is reflected in the functional changes in the resting state of the brain.

the motor learning process is associated with changes in the functional connectivity in the brain, in particular in the sensorimotor network, and that the changes can be functionally related to the motor or perceptual aspects of learning.
motor learning results in functionally-specific changes to distinct resting state networks in the brain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain is not a static entity, but instead, it changes its functional architecture in a functionally specific way in response to learning.

learning a new motor skill changes the brain's functional organization, with changes in functional connectivity between motor and sensory areas of the brain that are related to both motor and perceptual aspects of learning.
the functional connectivity of the brain changes in a functionally specific manner after learning, even under resting conditions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
learning changes not only the activity of motor and subcortex areas, as has been previously demonstrated, but also sensory networks in the brain.
motor learning changes the activity in both motor and somato-sensory networks in the brain.
the brain is not static but rather undergoes dynamic changes in response to learning.
